RUSSIAN-IRANIAN CASE, ¢| 

UPON A SOLUTION OF THAT PROBLEM, AT LEAST” FOR TIME BEING : |

THE PROBLEM, IN BRIEF. IS WHETHER THE COUNCIL WILL ACCEDE TO A 
VIGOROUS DEMAND BY RUSSIA THAT IT DROP IRAN FORTHWITH FROM ITS ‘AGENDA. 


THE IRANIANS HAVE FORMALLY WITHDRAWN THE COMPLAINT AGAINST RUSSIA 
WHICH THEY LODGED IN LONDON LAST@JAN, 18, THE RUSSIANS HAVE REPORTED 
AN AGREEMENT WITH IRAN AND HAVE DEMANDED THAT THE COUNCIL CEASE MAKING 
IRAN ITS BUSINESS. 

BUT THE COUNCIL APPARENTLY WILL SUSTAIN ITS ACTION OF APRIL 4 IN 
SHELVING THE*CASE UNTIL MAY 6,«AT WHICH TIME JT EXPECTS A REPORT 
WHETHER RUSSIA HAS COMPLETELY EVACUATED IRAN AS RUSSIA PROMISED. 

THE SECRETARY GENERAL OF THE UNITED ‘NATIONS, TRYGVE LIE 
A PRECEDENT LAST WEEK BY PRESENTING’ THE COUNCIL WITH AN UNSOLICITED 
RULING THAT THERE WAS SOME DOUBT WHETHER IT LEGALLY COULD RETAIN THE . 
CASE, SINCE IRAN HAD WITHDRAWN ITS COMPLAINT. THERE WAS SOME OPINION 
WITHIN THE COUNCIL THAT LIE HAD OVERSTEPPED HIS AUTHORITY BUT SOME 
OBSERVERS SAID LIE ACTED SOLELY TO FIND A WAY OUT OF THE IMPASSE. 

THE COUNCIL, ALMOST READY TO VOTE ON THE QUESTION, STALLED IT OFF 
FOR A WHILE BY PLACING THAT OPINION BEFORE ITS COMMITTEE OF EXPERTS 
FOR A RULING. THE COMMITTEE‘ REPORTED FORMALLY LAST. THURSDAY THAT IT 
WAS DIVIDED EIGHT. TO THREE IN FAVOR OF AN OPINION THAT THE COUNCIL 
COULD KEEP THE MATTER ON THE AGENDA, | 

THE EIGHT TO THREE SPLIT*IS THE SAME AS THAT IN, THE COUNCIL ITSELF, 
WITH RUSSIA, POLAND AND FRANCE STANDING ON THE MINORITY SIDE. 
OBSERVERS SAID THERE WAS A STRONG POSSIBILITY THAT A VOTE MIGHT BE 
TAKEN TUESDAY.

Critical of Stalin 
Trotsky writes in his introduc- 
tion that Stalin “is neither a think- 
er, a writér nor an orator” and that 
he “took possession of power, not 
with the aid of personal qualities, 
but with the aid of an impersonal 
machine.” 
*'He tells of Stalin’s birth as the 
son of a shoemaker in Georgia, and 
speculates on whether the Soviet 


grim through frightful beatings by 


of social inequality and finally, 
while a student in theological 
school, deserted religion and God. 


ary ideas. 

In summing up the Stalin of the 
order of professional revolution- 
ists, Trotsky says: 


“He saw the purpose of his life | 
in overthrowing the powers that be. | 


Hatred of them was immeasurably 


more active in his soul than love! 


for the oppressed. Prison, exile, sa- 
crifices, privations did not frighten 
him. He knew how to look danger 
straight in the eye. At the same 
time he was keenly sensitive about 
such of his traits as his slowness of 
intellect, lack of talent, the general 
colorlessness of his physical and 
moral countenance. His overween- 
ing ambition was tinged with envy 
and ill will. His pertinacity march- 
éd hand in hand with vindictive- 
ness.”

“I’m tremendously excited,”

of the quads, at her home in Hean-

Thompson Excited 

Thompson, now a commercial 
printer’s apprentice, said he was 
“happy and excited” but otherwise 
in “fine shape” and that he hoped 
to bring Miss Carpenter and the 
three children here by air for a 
marriage as quickly as possible. 

“I hope to marry her in Pitts- 
burgh but I’m not sure where or 
when,” he said. “I already have a 
four-room apartment promised me 
when I can get them here.” 

He already has sent the U.S. em- 
bassy in London a guarantee that 
he will support the family. He still 

as to send Miss Carpenter a copy 
of the divorce decree and a certifi- 


cate of intent to marry. She must 

present these papers to the em- 

bassy for approval of her trip.

Three Roads Lead to Peace 
Progress towara universal and 


constancy ‘te’ 


along three roads—onrganized 


international co-dépération, mu- 


tual international umderstand- 
ing and progressive ‘interna- 
tional disarmament. All must 
be traveled simultaneously. 

The first path, that of 
ganized intérnational co-opéra- 
tion, is undér survey by the. 


United Nations, That organiza-— 


must have our 
port, a support as tireless a 
effective as that which sus- 


through more than four yeats of 
bitter conflict..The United Na- 
tions eventually must guaran- 
tee, both to major and small 
powers, security against 
warranted infringement of na- 
tional rights—a common cause 


of war. 


In this hemisphere, we, with 
the other independent. nations 
ofthe Americas, have worked 


out relationships in which mu- 


tual co-operation for the solu- 
tion of common. problems is the 
keynote. We live by the. axiom 
that arbitration is a more efféc- 
tive means of settling’ disputes 
than is war. Years of develop= 
ment have been necessary to at- 
tain our present position, and 
while perféction has not ‘been 
attained, our degree of success 
is proof of the possibilities on a 

Progress along the second path 
—mutual international under- 
standing—is of particular sig- 
nificance because each of us, as 
individuals, can contribute to it. 
My own war experience with nu- 


meérous allies convinced me 


one fundamental truth in human - 
relations—that mutual knowl- 
edge tends to eliminate mu- 
tual fear, suspicion “and prej- 
udice, the prolific breeding 
grounds of dissension and quar- 
rels. Through every means open 
to us, we must strive for com- 
préhension of the history, the 
problems and the aspirations of 
others, just as we must assist 
others to gain similar compre- 
hension of ourselves. 
Vast Gulfs Separate Peoples 
Vast guifs of social, economic 
and political differencés still 
separate the peoples of the earth. 
Centuries and generations have 
gone into their.development. We 
cannot expect to bridge them 
by wishful thinking or to abol- 
ish them in a few conferencés. 
Again, our own ‘conception of 
democracy, no matter, how.earn- 


estly venerated by ourselves, is 


of little importance to. men 
whose immediaté.concern is the 
preservation of physical life. 
With famine and.starvation the 
lot of half the ‘world, food is of 
fai more current nce to
